books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

primary_sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854)
Henry David Thoreau, "Resistance to Civil Government," 1849

stimulus.text: The portrait shows Henry David Thoreau as a bearded man in a dark jacket and bow tie, looking straight at the camera. It is a daguerreotype made in 1856, two years after he published Walden; or, Life in the Woods, his account of the two years he lived alone in a cabin at Walden Pond outside Concord, Massachusetts. Thoreau also wrote the essay "Resistance to Civil Government" (1849), urging readers not to obey unjust government orders.
stimulus.source_note: Description records only what the portrait visibly shows; the facts about Walden Pond and the 1849 essay come from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.10, Transcendentalism. Portrait: daguerreotype of Henry David Thoreau by Benjamin D. Maxham, 1856, public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus describes a public-domain 1856 daguerreotype of Thoreau
stem: Thoreau's two years at Walden Pond most directly illustrate which transcendentalist idea?

options.text: That wealth and factory work are the best measures of a good life
options.misconception: The market revolution rewarded wealth, so a famous writer's life can look like praise of getting rich.

options.text: That the federal government should build canals and railroads across the West
options.misconception: Canals and railroads were the era's great projects, so any 1840s figure seems tied to them.

options.text: That churches and ministers are the only reliable guides to truth
options.misconception: Thoreau wrote about spiritual things, so his guide to truth can look like the church.

options.text: That a person finds meaning by living simply and experiencing nature directly

rationales.A: Thoreau lived simply on purpose, rejecting the market's measure of people by output and wealth. His cabin was a protest against that measure.
rationales.B: Thoreau wrote about a cabin and a pond, not about canals or railroads. Internal improvements were a political program, not his subject.
rationales.C: Transcendentalists trusted intuition and nature over churches and tradition. Thoreau went to the woods precisely to find truth outside the church.
rationales.D: Walden Pond was the experiment: two years of simple living in nature, testing whether direct experience teaches what institutions cannot.
rationales.general:
1. Read the experiment: a cabin, a pond, two years alone, and a book about it.
2. Ask what he was testing: whether simple living and nature teach more than routine work and church doctrine.
3. Name the idea: meaning comes from direct experience, not from institutions or wealth.
Background: Thoreau lived at Walden Pond from 1845 to 1847 and published Walden in 1854.
Remember: when a writer moves to the woods, ask what he is walking away from.
